paragraphs: The paper studies how a network of computing nodes can jointly optimize a shared objective when each node knows only its own local cost. Those costs are smooth but nonconvex, and nodes receive noisy gradient information. The target is an approximately stationary point, where the combined objective has a sufficiently small gradient.

The proposed method, GT-HSGD, combines local estimators that reduce gradient noise with communication that tracks the global gradient across the network. It uses a single optimization loop. This design connects two difficulties: making useful progress from noisy local information and coordinating that progress toward the sum of all local costs.

For sufficiently small error tolerance epsilon, the method achieves an oracle complexity of O(n^-1 epsilon^-3), independent of network topology. The authors interpret this as linear speedup with the number of nodes relative to optimal centralized online variance-reduced methods using one node. The small-tolerance qualification matters to that result. Numerical experiments illustrate the theory, while the paper also reports advantages in practical implementation.
icml-2021-a-hybrid-variance-reduced-meth.tldr: GT-HSGD combines local variance reduction and network gradient tracking to achieve conditional linear speedup in decentralized stochastic optimization.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the problem of generating a molecule’s three-dimensional structure from its molecular graph. A common approach first predicts distances between atoms and then solves a geometry problem to place those atoms in space. The authors identify a weakness in this separation: predicted distances may fail to consistently preserve the geometry of local atomic neighborhoods.

Their method, ConfVAE, brings conformation generation into an end-to-end framework based on a conditional variational autoencoder. It first encodes the molecular graph into a latent representation. It then generates three-dimensional structures by solving a bilevel optimization problem, linking the representation stage with the optimization used to construct molecular geometry.

The approach matters because its learning framework connects molecular information to the final structural output, addressing the disconnect identified in two-stage prediction. Experiments across several benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness relative to existing leading approaches. These findings support the proposed framework as a useful way to generate conformations; they are empirical evidence for its performance on the evaluated molecular structure tasks.
icml-2021-an-end-to-end-framework-for-mo.tldr: ConfVAE connects molecular graph encoding and three-dimensional structure generation through an end-to-end bilevel optimization framework.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether batch reinforcement learning can recover the optimal action-value function, Q*, from a polynomial-sized exploratory dataset with a very weak requirement on the candidate functions. That requirement, realizability, says the function class contains Q*. Beyond this, the class may be arbitrary. Earlier algorithms required stronger function-approximation assumptions, contributing to a conjecture that efficient learning under realizability alone was impossible.

The proposed algorithm, BVFT, organizes learning as a tournament between candidate functions. Instead of directly solving the entire selection problem, it compares candidates in pairs. Each comparison uses a partition of the state-action space constructed from the two functions being compared.

The result challenges the hardness conjecture while retaining an important qualification: BVFT requires a stronger notion of exploratory data. Thus, the progress comes from weakening assumptions on the function class while relying on stronger data exploration. The paper also discusses applying the tournament approach to model selection. Its central contribution is a new route to sample-efficient learning under this particular combination of assumptions.
icml-2021-batch-value-function-approxima.tldr: BVFT learns through pairwise function comparisons under realizability alone, provided the batch data satisfy a stronger exploration requirement.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction tasks whose outputs must obey structural rules, such as translating pseudocode into code that compiles. Paired training examples can be expensive, while outputs without corresponding inputs may be plentiful. Training a denoiser to reconstruct corrupted outputs lets a model learn information about valid output structure from this unpaired material.

The authors show that ordinary fine-tuning can destroy some of the structure acquired during pre-training. Their composed fine-tuning method trains a predictor together with a fixed pre-trained denoiser in a composed system. The predictor is also initialized from the denoiser, but the denoiser itself remains frozen to preserve its learned structural information.

For two-layer ReLU networks, the paper proves that this construction reduces predictor complexity and improves generalization. On two pseudocode-to-code datasets, it reports relative improvements of 3% and 6% over standard fine-tuning. The corresponding improvements on out-of-distribution examples are 4% and 25%. These results suggest that reducing predictor complexity can help extrapolation beyond the training distribution.
icml-2021-composed-fine-tuning-freezing-.tldr: Composed fine-tuning preserves learned output structure with a frozen denoiser and improves generalization in pseudocode-to-code experiments.

paragraphs: Predicting a time series often calls for an interval expressing uncertainty around each forecast. This paper introduces EnbPI, which constructs such intervals sequentially around any bootstrap ensemble estimator. It is closely connected to conformal prediction, but does not require exchangeability of the data, a condition that is restrictive for observations ordered through time.

The theoretical result establishes approximately valid marginal coverage at finite sample sizes for broad classes of regression functions and time series with strongly mixing stochastic errors. Both qualifications matter: coverage is approximate and marginal, and the result assumes a particular form of dependence in the errors. Removing exchangeability therefore does not remove all conditions on the time series.

Computationally, EnbPI aggregates bootstrap estimators that have already been trained. It avoids data splitting and does not require training multiple separate ensemble estimators. The authors describe it as scalable to an arbitrary number of sequential intervals and report extensive real-data analyses supporting its effectiveness. The contribution combines a qualified coverage guarantee with a practical way to reuse an existing prediction ensemble.
icml-2021-conformal-prediction-interval-.tldr: EnbPI efficiently produces sequential prediction intervals with approximately valid marginal coverage under stated time-series dependence conditions.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines contributions from multiple clients into a shared model. Malicious clients can exploit that process through poisoned data or model replacement, introducing backdoors into the resulting model. This paper addresses a gap between defenses that perform well in experiments and defenses that provide a mathematical robustness certificate.

The proposed framework, CRFL, applies clipping and smoothing to model parameters to control the smoothness of the global model. This yields robustness certificates for individual samples against backdoors of limited magnitude. The guarantee is therefore tied to a bounded attack setting and is expressed at the sample level.

The certification also describes how robustness relates to features of federated training, including the fraction of poisoned instances, the number of attackers, and the number of training iterations. This connects the guarantee to the process that produces the shared model. Experiments across federated datasets accompany the framework, and the authors introduce a benchmark for certified backdoor robustness. The contribution is both a certification method and an empirical basis for studying these guarantees.
icml-2021-crfl-certifiably-robust-federa.tldr: CRFL uses parameter clipping and smoothing to certify sample-level robustness against bounded backdoor attacks in federated learning.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning asks an agent to maximize expected total reward while meeting constraints on expected total costs. Both the reward objective and multiple constraints can be nonconvex, making global optimization difficult. Many existing methods handle the constraints by maintaining additional dual variables alongside the policy.

Constraint-rectified policy optimization, or CRPO, instead directly alternates policy updates between improving the objective and satisfying constraints. Its framework can accommodate different policy optimization steps. This makes the policy itself the focus of both reward improvement and constraint correction, without the primal-dual structure used by the compared approaches.

For the version using natural policy gradient updates, the authors prove convergence to a globally optimal policy within the constrained policy set at rate O(1/sqrt(T)). They also obtain an O(1/sqrt(T)) bound on constraint-satisfaction error. These guarantees apply to that analyzed update choice, rather than automatically to every variant the framework can accept. Experiments show that CRPO can substantially outperform the evaluated primal-dual baselines, complementing the finite-time theoretical analysis.
icml-2021-crpo-a-new-approach-for-safe-r.tldr: CRPO alternates reward improvement and constraint correction, with global convergence and constraint-error guarantees for natural policy gradient updates.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples alongside labeled data, often by assigning predictions as temporary labels. The paper identifies a problem with two common selection strategies: using every unlabeled example or accepting only predictions above a fixed confidence threshold. Either strategy can discard useful correct pseudo-labels or include too many incorrect ones.

Dash adds an adaptive selection mechanism to existing semi-supervised methods. At each update, it retains unlabeled examples only when their losses fall below a threshold that changes over training. The intended selection favors pseudo-labels related to the labeled data, making the choice of training examples responsive to the learning process.

The authors establish a convergence rate for Dash through an analysis of nonconvex optimization. They also evaluate it against leading methods on benchmark tasks and report evidence of effectiveness. The contribution links a simple, changing loss cutoff with theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation. Its significance is the ability to adapt which unlabeled examples influence learning as training progresses, rather than committing to one fixed selection rule throughout.
icml-2021-dash-semi-supervised-learning-.tldr: Dash adaptively selects pseudo-labeled examples using a changing loss threshold, with convergence analysis and supporting benchmark results.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning in environments that continue changing over an agent’s lifetime. Typical formulations instead assume the decision process stays fixed across episodes. Persistent change creates a particular difficulty for off-policy learning, which reuses past experiences: those experiences may have been collected under different environmental conditions.

The authors formalize this setting and derive an off-policy algorithm using ideas from online learning and probabilistic inference. A latent variable model learns a representation of the environment from both current and past experiences. The reinforcement learning algorithm then uses this representation, giving it a mechanism for reasoning about environmental change while still drawing on earlier data.

The paper also introduces simulation environments with lifelong non-stationarity. In those evaluations, the method substantially outperforms approaches that do not reason about environment shifts. This is an empirical finding in the introduced settings. It supports the value of explicitly representing change when reusing experience, and makes continual adaptation part of the learning problem rather than assuming a fixed environment.
icml-2021-deep-reinforcement-learning-am.tldr: A latent-variable off-policy reinforcement learning method reasons about persistent environment changes and improves performance in non-stationary simulations.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning must learn from data whose distribution differs from the distribution associated with the policy being optimized. Actor-critic methods can correct this mismatch using estimated density ratios. However, errors in those ratios and in the estimated value function can introduce substantial bias into the updates.

The paper proposes DR-Off-PAC, a doubly robust actor-critic method for discounted Markov decision processes. It uses learned auxiliary functions to reduce estimation errors. The actor and critics update simultaneously on a single timescale with constant stepsizes, avoiding the two-timescale or nested-loop organization used by prior algorithms discussed in the paper.

The authors analyze finite-time convergence and the number of samples needed to obtain an epsilon-accurate optimal policy. They also establish double robustness of overall convergence to approximation errors associated with the expressive power of the chosen function approximators. The contribution brings robustness analysis together with a simpler update schedule, which the paper identifies as more sample efficient than those prior structures. Its guarantees explicitly account for function-approximation error.
icml-2021-doubly-robust-off-policy-actor.tldr: DR-Off-PAC combines doubly robust estimation with simultaneous actor-critic updates and analyzes its convergence, sample complexity, and approximation errors.

paragraphs: Image classifiers commonly learn visual representations while treating class descriptions as fixed one-hot codes. The authors argue that this separation limits the search for shared visual properties and the recognition of unseen samples. They draw inspiration from concept formation, where discovering common properties and developing descriptions of concepts proceed together.

Their strategy, LSOVCF, jointly learns feature extraction and concept descriptions within a convolutional network. It uses responses from the network’s final layer to infer concept descriptions, assuming those descriptions take the form of Gaussian distributions. An exploration-and-experience loss guides optimization, and an experience cache pool is used to accelerate convergence.

Experiments report improved recognition of unseen samples on CIFAR-10, STL10, Flower17, and ImageNet across several network backbones, including VGG and GhostNet. These results support learning the representation and its concept descriptions together in the evaluated classification settings. The Gaussian assumption is a concrete part of how the method represents concepts, while the empirical contribution shows that the strategy can benefit multiple underlying convolutional architectures.
icml-2021-explore-visual-concept-formati.tldr: LSOVCF jointly learns visual features and Gaussian concept descriptions, improving unseen-sample recognition across several image-classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper considers adapting word embeddings to a new domain when very little text is available. Its guiding intuition is that only a small subset of words may need substantially different embeddings, such as words that acquire a new meaning in that domain. This creates an opportunity to transfer existing representations while concentrating adaptation on selected words.

The authors develop a group-sparse penalty for low-rank matrix factorization, the framework they use to learn embeddings from unstructured text. The penalty exploits sparsity in which words change during transfer. This extends ideas from sparse regression into unsupervised representation learning and targets settings with as little target-domain text as a single article.

The paper proves generalization bounds for the algorithm and evaluates it empirically through downstream prediction accuracy and interpretability. Those two evaluation perspectives address both the usefulness of the adapted embeddings and the understandability of the changes. The approach matters when limited target data make selective adaptation appealing, with the expectation of sparse word-level changes providing its central structural motivation.
icml-2021-group-sparse-matrix-factorizat.tldr: A group-sparse matrix-factorization method adapts word embeddings from very little target text by exploiting selective word-level changes.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a learning setting motivated by a prosthetic arm adapting to its user’s control signals. The learner receives a context vector, chooses an action, and observes a feedback vector. Crucially, that feedback does not explicitly identify a reward, so the learner cannot directly use the reward signal assumed by common reinforcement learning methods.

Interaction-Grounded Learning makes discovering how to evaluate feedback part of the task. The agent must uncover a latent reward signal and use it to ground its policy without supervision. This links two learning problems: interpreting what feedback means for successful interaction and choosing actions based on that interpretation.

The authors show that this is possible under certain natural assumptions in their proposed setting. They provide theoretical guarantees and a proof-of-concept empirical evaluation. The result is conditional on those assumptions; it does not claim that arbitrary feedback always reveals a useful reward. Its contribution is to formalize and demonstrate a route to learning successful interactions when rewards are implicit in multidimensional feedback.
icml-2021-interaction-grounded-learning-.tldr: Interaction-Grounded Learning discovers a latent reward from feedback without explicit reward labels, with guarantees under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Some data lie on geometric spaces such as a torus or a group of rotations. The paper addresses statistical testing on these Riemannian manifolds, where ordinary multivariate procedures do not directly apply. Its goal is to assess whether a proposed probability distribution fits the observed data and to support interpretable criticism of that model.

The authors extend kernel Stein discrepancy using Stein operators defined on Riemannian manifolds. These extensions provide a geometry-aware basis for goodness-of-fit tests. The methods cover general distributions on these spaces, including distributions whose normalization constants are intractable, broadening the models that can be assessed within the framework.

The paper relates its tests to existing approaches and analyzes their asymptotic Bahadur efficiency, a theoretical measure of testing efficiency as sample sizes grow. Simulations and real-data applications support the methods’ validity and usefulness. Together, these contributions connect statistical model checking with the geometry of the data, while combining formal efficiency analysis with evidence from practical applications.
icml-2021-interpretable-stein-goodness-o.tldr: Geometry-aware Stein tests assess and interpret distributional fit on Riemannian manifolds, including models with intractable normalization constants.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can require substantial computation because candidate networks are trained before being evaluated. This paper seeks to reduce that search cost and its associated environmental burden by assessing architectures without training them. The central question is whether information available at random initialization can provide a useful indication of later performance.

The authors propose the gradient kernel hypothesis: gradients induced by an architecture can act as a coarse proxy for downstream training. They provide theoretical analysis and identify a practical gradient kernel that correlates well with training loss and validation performance. KNAS uses this kernel to guide architecture search, treating the gradient signal as an approximate evaluation tool.

On image-classification tasks, experiments show competitive results with search running orders of magnitude faster than train-then-test approaches. A searched network also outperforms RoBERTa-large on two text-classification tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the proxy in the evaluated settings. The environmental motivation is addressed through reduced search computation; the reported evidence concerns search speed and predictive performance.
icml-2021-knas-green-neural-architecture.tldr: KNAS uses gradient kernels at random initialization to search architectures without candidate training, greatly reducing search time in experiments.

paragraphs: In convex optimization with feedback, a learner repeatedly submits queries and uses the responses to approach a function’s minimizer. Those queries can also reveal information to an eavesdropper. This paper studies how to obscure the query sequence so that the learner’s learned optimum remains difficult for an observer to estimate accurately.

The authors consider two privacy formulations. In the Bayesian formulation, the convex function is drawn randomly. In the minimax formulation, it is fixed and the adversary’s estimation performance is evaluated through a minimax criterion. The learner receives first-order feedback, including full gradients, which makes the setting richer than earlier sequential learning models with binary feedback.

The main finding distinguishes the cost of privacy in these formulations. To keep the adversary’s probability of accurate estimation below 1/L, query-complexity overhead is additive in L for minimax privacy but multiplicative in L for Bayesian privacy. The proof uses Dirichlet-process tools and information-leakage analysis for full-gradient feedback. The result shows that the chosen privacy formulation materially changes the optimization effort required.
icml-2021-learner-private-convex-optimiz.tldr: The query cost of hiding a convex optimizer’s learned optimum scales differently under Bayesian and minimax privacy formulations.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning in mean-field games, where a Nash equilibrium includes both a policy and a mean-field state describing the population. Existing algorithms require finding an optimal policy while holding a mean-field state fixed. That requirement separates learning from play, although in practice agents learn while the population state is changing.

The authors propose a fictitious play algorithm that alternates small updates to both components. It takes one policy optimization step for learning and one gradient descent step for updating the mean-field state. This avoids requiring a completed policy optimization before the population state can move again.

Alternating these updates introduces nonstationarity because each component evolves as the other is being learned. Despite that moving target, the paper proves convergence to the Nash equilibrium and gives an explicit convergence rate. The authors describe this as the first provably efficient approach achieving learning while playing through alternating updates. The contribution establishes that joint ongoing adaptation can be analyzed directly, rather than relying on a fixed population state during policy learning.
icml-2021-learning-while-playing-in-mean.tldr: An alternating fictitious play algorithm learns policies while updating the mean-field state, with a proved rate of convergence to equilibrium.

paragraphs: Batch policy optimization builds a policy from existing data before further interaction with an environment. This paper studies its theoretical limits in stochastic bandits with finitely many actions. It introduces confidence-adjusted index algorithms, placing optimistic, pessimistic, and neutral approaches within one framework so their guarantees can be analyzed together.

Every algorithm in this family is minimax optimal, meaning that the worst-case criterion does not distinguish those different attitudes toward uncertainty. The authors also show that instance-dependent optimality, useful in online bandit analysis, cannot be achieved by any batch algorithm. An algorithm that is optimal in one environment can incur arbitrarily larger regret in another.

To distinguish algorithms more meaningfully, the paper introduces a weighted-minimax criterion incorporating the inherent difficulty of predicting the optimal value. Under this perspective, the authors show how commonly used pessimistic principles can be justified. The contribution therefore concerns both algorithms and evaluation: ordinary worst-case optimality groups several approaches together, while the new criterion provides a basis for explaining why pessimism can be appropriate.
icml-2021-on-the-optimality-of-batch-pol.tldr: Batch bandit optimality requires careful evaluation criteria: a new weighted-minimax perspective can justify pessimism where ordinary minimax optimality cannot distinguish approaches.

paragraphs: This paper examines how graph neural networks train, complementing work on what they can represent and how they generalize. The authors study gradient dynamics to understand whether optimization converges and which architectural or data-related properties affect its speed. Their theoretical starting point is a class of linearized graph neural networks.

For these models, the paper proves convergence to a global minimum at a linear rate despite the nonconvex training problem. The result holds under mild assumptions that the authors validate on real-world graphs. Their analysis further identifies skip connections, greater depth, and a favorable label distribution as factors that can implicitly accelerate training.

Experiments show that the theoretical behavior of the linearized models aligns with observed training behavior in nonlinear graph neural networks. This provides empirical support for the relevance of the analysis beyond its formal model class. The findings give an optimization-based explanation for the success of skip connections and suggest practical promise for deeper networks that use them, while keeping the formal convergence guarantee tied to the analyzed assumptions and models.
icml-2021-optimization-of-graph-neural-n.tldr: Analysis of linearized graph neural networks explains how skip connections, depth, and label distribution can accelerate training.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient noise influences both optimization and generalization in deep learning. The paper emphasizes that this noise varies by direction and depends on model parameters, so injecting simple random noise does not reproduce its behavior well. The authors seek a low-cost way to manipulate stochastic gradient noise without changing the learning rate or batch size.

Positive-Negative Momentum, or PNM, maintains two approximately independent momentum terms. Adjusting their difference provides explicit control over the noise magnitude. The mechanism serves as an alternative to conventional momentum and can be incorporated into familiar optimizers, connecting noise control to the optimizer’s existing treatment of gradient information.

The paper provides a convergence guarantee and a theoretical generalization advantage over stochastic gradient descent. It also incorporates PNM into momentum SGD and Adam. Extensive experiments report significant advantages over the corresponding conventional-momentum versions. These findings support momentum design as a means of shaping the noise involved in learning, with both theoretical analysis and empirical comparisons motivating the proposed replacement.
icml-2021-positive-negative-momentum-man.tldr: Positive-Negative Momentum controls stochastic gradient noise through two momentum terms, with theoretical and empirical evidence of improved generalization.

paragraphs: The paper revisits whether matrix-factorization collaborative filtering is preferable to neural collaborative filtering. Earlier empirical observations favored matrix factorization and suggested that a dot product might be a better similarity function than a feed-forward network. The authors investigate that comparison through representational capacity, gradient-descent optimization, and generalization.

Their results show similar expressivity for overparameterized versions of the two model families when viewed as kernelized predictors. They also reveal a relationship between their optimization paths. This connects the models at the level of what they can express and how training proceeds, rather than judging them only through observed predictive performance.

Generalization produces a more differentiated picture, with tradeoffs across inductive and transductive collaborative filtering settings. The paper additionally establishes a result highlighting the importance of correcting exposure bias when evaluating models in the inductive setting. Synthetic and real-data experiments provide further insight. Together, the findings explain some earlier conflicting observations and make the comparison depend on the learning and evaluation setting, rather than establishing one model family as universally superior.
icml-2021-rethinking-neural-vs-matrix-fa.tldr: Theory links neural and matrix-factorization recommenders while revealing setting-dependent generalization tradeoffs and the importance of correcting exposure bias.

paragraphs: Understanding and correcting a recurrent neural network’s mistakes is difficult because its predictions depend on internal state as well as the sequence it processes. RNNRepair addresses this problem with a lightweight model-based analysis. It constructs an influence model describing the network’s stateful and statistical behavior across the training data.

The model estimates how training examples affect a particular prediction, considering both complete samples and segments within sequences. It can analyze existing training examples as well as newly added ones. This finer-grained view connects an incorrect prediction to potentially influential training material without treating every sequence as an indivisible unit.

The empirical evaluation finds that the influence model extracts accurate, understandable features and can identify influential instances for entire test sequences or particular segments. The authors then use these influence relations to remediate two types of incorrect predictions at the sample and segment levels. The contribution connects interpretation with repair: the same analysis that helps explain a mistake also supplies relationships used to address it in the evaluated settings.
icml-2021-rnnrepair-automatic-rnn-repair.tldr: RNNRepair models training-data influence at sequence and segment levels to help explain and repair recurrent-network prediction errors.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning representations of whole graphs without supervision, a task relevant to applications such as predicting molecular properties. The authors identify a gap in methods that preserve local similarities between graph instances: these methods may fail to uncover the broader semantic organization of the dataset.

GraphLoG combines local-instance learning with global-semantic learning. It retains information about nearby or similar graph instances while introducing hierarchical prototypes to represent semantic clusters across the dataset. An efficient online expectation-maximization algorithm learns the model. The local and global components therefore provide complementary structure for organizing whole-graph representations during training.

The evaluation pre-trains GraphLoG on a large collection of unlabeled graphs and then fine-tunes the learned model for downstream tasks. Experiments on chemical and biological benchmarks support its effectiveness. These findings suggest that representation learning can benefit from capturing dataset-wide groupings alongside local similarities. The contribution lies in a unified framework that makes both forms of structure part of self-supervised learning, with an online procedure for fitting the model.
icml-2021-self-supervised-graph-level-re.tldr: GraphLoG learns whole-graph representations by combining local similarities with hierarchical prototypes of global semantic clusters.

paragraphs: Airline crew scheduling requires predictions that fit together under operational constraints. This paper introduces structured convolutional kernel networks, or Struct-CKN, to support that requirement. Convolutional kernel networks approximate a kernel feature map from training data, bringing together properties of convolutional learning and the flexibility of kernel methods.

The authors extend these networks to structured prediction with constrained outputs. A flight-based network is represented through a general conditional random field, allowing local constraints to enter the learning process. The resulting predictions provide useful initial solutions on flight-connection data, which an airline crew scheduling solver can then refine.

Experiments address a large-scale crew pairing problem involving 50,000 flights per month. Relative to standard approaches, the method reduces solution cost by 17%, described as a gain of millions of dollars, and reduces the cost of global constraints by 97%. These are reported results for the evaluated scheduling application. The contribution shows how constraint-aware learned initial solutions can improve a workflow that includes subsequent refinement by a specialized solver.
icml-2021-structured-convolutional-kerne.tldr: Struct-CKN produces constraint-aware initial crew schedules that improve solver outcomes, including a reported 17% reduction in solution cost.

paragraphs: Adversarial training improves resistance to adversarial examples, but this paper finds that its benefits can be distributed unevenly across data groups. The authors examine disparities in both ordinary accuracy and adversarial robustness. The issue can appear even in balanced datasets, so equal class representation alone does not resolve the observed problem.

For a PGD-trained ResNet18 on CIFAR-10, the abstract reports clean accuracy of 93% for automobiles and 65% for cats, with adversarial accuracy of 67% and 17%, respectively. These examples illustrate how aggregate robustness can coexist with substantial class-level differences. The authors provide empirical and theoretical evidence that such disparities can arise more generally when adversarial training minimizes robust error.

The paper proposes Fair-Robust-Learning, or FRL, to mitigate this unfairness during adversarial defense. Experiments validate the framework’s effectiveness. Here, fairness concerns the distribution of accuracy and robustness across groups of data, including image classes. The contribution highlights a consequence of adversarial training and offers a framework for addressing that uneven performance.
icml-2021-to-be-robust-or-to-be-fair-tow.tldr: Adversarial training can create large class-level accuracy and robustness gaps, and FRL mitigates these disparities in experiments.
